Real Property vs. Personal Property▾
The three layers: land, real estate, real property

Build the vocabulary first. Land is the earth's surface, everything beneath it down to the center of the earth, and the air space above it. Real estate is land plus everything permanently attached to it, whether by nature (trees, minerals) or by people (a house, a fence). Real property is real estate plus the legal bundle of rights of ownership; the rights to possess, use, exclude, encumber, and dispose. Personal property (also called chattel) is everything movable that is not permanently attached.

How things change category: annexation and severance

Property is not stuck in one category forever. Annexation (attachment) is the act of permanently attaching personal property to land so that it becomes real property; a pile of loose bricks (personal) built into a permanent garden wall (real). Severance is the reverse: detaching something from the land so that it becomes personal property; an apple growing on a tree is real property, but once picked it is personal property; a chandelier is real property until it is unscrewed and boxed to keep.

Deed vs. bill of sale
Two different documents move the two different kinds of property. A deed transfers real property (the land and whatever is permanently attached). A bill of sale transfers personal property (movable items). When a home sells, the house passes by deed; a washer, dryer, or patio set that goes with it should be listed and passed by a bill of sale.
Fixtures and the MARIA test

A fixture is personal property that has become real property through attachment. Whether an item counts as a fixture is judged by five factors, remembered as MARIA:

MMethod of attachment
AAdaptability to the property
RRelationship of the parties
IIntention of the person
AAgreement between the parties
Trade fixtures
Items a tenant attaches to run a business; display shelving, a barber's chair, a bakery's ovens; are trade fixtures and remain the tenant's personal property. The tenant may remove them before the lease ends. If left behind, they become the landlord's by accession.

Emblements are annual crops produced by a tenant farmer's labor (corn, wheat). They remain the tenant's personal property, so the tenant may return to harvest even after the lease term ends.

💡
Two anchors for this whole lesson: in MARIA, a written Agreement is the tie-breaker that beats every other factor; and deed = real property, bill of sale = personal property.
🎯
Real property (passes by deed): a chandelier, a built-in bookcase or dishwasher, a planted shrub. Personal property (passes by bill of sale): a potted plant, an area rug, a free-standing refrigerator, a window A/C unit that slides out. Annual crops are emblements; personal property of the tenant who grew them.
Physical & Economic Characteristics of Real Property▾
Why land behaves unlike anything else

Real estate has a fixed set of physical traits (what land is) and economic traits (what land is worth). There are seven in all; three physical and four economic. Learn them as the nature of land itself.

Physical characteristics — what land IS

Immobility. The geographic location of a parcel can never be moved. You can haul away soil, but the parcel stays where it is. Synonyms you may see: fixed location. Consequence: real estate law and records are local, tied to where the land sits.

Indestructibility. Land is durable and permanent; it cannot be destroyed. Improvements can burn or crumble, but the land endures. Synonyms: durability, permanence.

Non-homogeneity. No two parcels are exactly alike; at the very least, each occupies a different location. Synonyms: uniqueness, heterogeneity, nonhomogeneity. Consequence: because each parcel is unique, a wronged buyer can seek specific performance rather than settle for money.

Economic characteristics — what land is WORTH

Scarcity. The overall supply of land; especially usable, well-located land; is limited, which supports value.

Improvement (modification). Improvements to and on the land change its value and use, and one owner's improvement can raise or lower a neighbor's value.

Permanence of investment (fixity). Money and labor invested in land and buildings are fixed and long-term; the return comes slowly over many years. Synonyms: fixity of investment.

Area preference (situs). People's preference for one location over another. Situs is the economic desirability of a location and is often called the single most important economic characteristic; it is the real meaning of “location, location, location.”

CharacteristicTypePlain meaningAlso called
ImmobilityPhysicalLocation can't be movedFixed location
IndestructibilityPhysicalLand can't be destroyedDurability, permanence
Non-homogeneityPhysicalEvery parcel is uniqueUniqueness, heterogeneity
ScarcityEconomicUsable land is limitedLimited supply
ImprovementEconomicChanges value & useModification
Permanence of investmentEconomicCapital is fixed, long-termFixity
Area preferenceEconomicDesirability of locationSitus
💡
CRESS memory device; “The 3 & the 4.” Three physical traits describe land's body: it is Immovable, Indestructible, and Unique (I·I·U). Four economic traits describe its wallet: Scarcity, Improvement, Permanence, Area preference (S·I·P·A; and the A is situs).
🎯
Do not confuse these seven with DUST. DUST (Demand, Utility, Scarcity, Transferability) lists the characteristics of value and belongs to the valuation/appraisal curriculum. The seven here are the characteristics of land itself. Scarcity appears in both ideas; read whether the question asks about land's nature (these seven) or value (DUST).
Legal Descriptions▾
Why a street address is not enough

A mailing or street address can be renumbered, duplicated in another town, or simply fail to fix a boundary. To convey real property, a document needs a legal description; a precise, legally sufficient way to identify the exact parcel. Three methods do this job.

1) Metes and Bounds

This method traces the boundary by distances (metes) and directions and boundaries (bounds). It starts at a point of beginning (POB), follows each call in turn using monuments (natural or artificial markers such as an iron pin or a creek), directions, and distances, and must return to the point of beginning so the boundary closes. It is ideal for irregular parcels.

Worked example
“Beginning at the iron pin at the northeast corner of Oak Street and Main Street; thence north 100 feet; thence east 80 feet; thence south 100 feet; thence west 80 feet to the point of beginning.” If the calls did not return to the POB, the description would not close and would be defective.
2) Government (Rectangular) Survey System

This system maps land using principal meridians (north-south reference lines) and baselines (east-west reference lines). Land is divided into townships. A range is a column of townships running east or west of a meridian; a tier is a row of townships running north or south of a baseline.

UnitSizeKey relationship
Township6 miles × 6 milesContains 36 sections
Section1 mile × 1 mileContains 640 acres
Half section—320 acres
Quarter section—160 acres
Acre—43,560 square feet
3) Lot and Block (Recorded Plat)

A subdivider divides land and records a plat map that lays out numbered lots within blocks in a named subdivision. Once the plat is recorded in the public records, any parcel can be described simply by its lot number, block number, subdivision name, and recording reference. This is the common method for residential subdivisions.

Surveys

A survey is prepared by a licensed surveyor to establish or confirm the exact boundaries of a parcel, locate the improvements on it, and reveal problems such as encroachments or easements. In short, a survey shows where the lines truly fall on the ground.

💡
Three ways to describe land, remembered as M-G-L: Metes & bounds (POB → back to POB), Government survey (meridians, baselines, townships, 640-acre sections), and Lot & block (a recorded plat). A street address alone is not a legal description.
🎯
Memorize the survey math: a section = 640 acres; a township = 36 sections and is 6 miles square; a quarter-section = 160 acres; one acre = 43,560 sq ft. To size a nested description, multiply the fractions: the quarter of a quarter section = 1/16 of 640 = 40 acres.
Public & Private Land Use Controls & Encumbrances▾
Two kinds of control: public and private

Every parcel is subject to limits. Public controls come from the powers of government. Private controls come from agreements and restrictions created by owners. Knowing which is which is a frequent exam skill.

Public controls — PETE and zoning

Government keeps four powers over private land, remembered as PETE:

PPolice power
EEminent domain
TTaxation
EEscheat

Police power is the authority to regulate for public health, safety, and welfare; the source of zoning ordinances, building codes, and setbacks. It requires no compensation. Eminent domain is the power to take private property for public use, and it does require just compensation; the legal process used to take it is condemnation. When government effectively takes or ruins a parcel without formally condemning it, the owner may sue in inverse condemnation to force a purchase. Taxation funds government through real estate taxes; unpaid taxes become a tax lien. Escheat returns property to the state when an owner dies with no heirs and no will.

Zoning tools to know
A variance is permission to deviate from a zoning rule because strict enforcement would cause a hardship (for example, an oddly shaped lot). A nonconforming use is a use that was lawful before the zoning changed and is allowed to continue; often called being grandfathered. A conditional (special) use permit allows a use the zone permits only under stated conditions.
Private controls — CC&Rs, deed restrictions, HOAs

Deed restrictions and restrictive covenants; often bundled as CC&Rs (Covenants, Conditions & Restrictions); are private limits a developer or owner places in a deed or a recorded declaration (for example, a minimum home size, or no commercial use). A homeowners association (HOA) enforces the CC&Rs and collects dues. These are enforced by other owners or the HOA, not by the government. When a public rule and a private restriction both apply, the stricter of the two generally controls.

Encumbrances: easements, licenses, encroachments

An easement is a right to use another's land. An easement appurtenant benefits an adjoining parcel and runs with the land to future owners; an easement in gross benefits a person or company (a utility line). A license is mere temporary, revocable permission to use land; it is not an interest in the land and can be withdrawn at will. An encroachment is an unauthorized physical intrusion, such as a fence or roofline built across the boundary.

Public controlPrivate control
SourceGovernment power (PETE, zoning)Owner agreements (CC&Rs, deeds)
ExamplesZoning, eminent domain, taxesDeed restrictions, HOA rules
Enforced byThe governmentOther owners or the HOA
Compensation?Only for eminent domainNot applicable
💡
Public = PETE + zoning (government; only eminent domain pays compensation). Private = CC&Rs / deed restrictions / HOAs (agreements). For use rights: an easement is an interest that can run with the land; a license is revocable permission; an encroachment is an unwanted intrusion.
🎯
High-yield contrasts: eminent domain requires just compensation, police-power zoning does not. A variance = deviation for hardship; a nonconforming use = grandfathered prior use. When public zoning and private CC&Rs conflict, the stricter rule wins. A license can be revoked; an easement generally cannot.

The official Pearson VUE national content outline allocates about 9 of the 80 scored questions to this section. These are outline weightings, not a guarantee of specific questions.

Cognitive weighting
Knowledge5
Application2

Ownership, Estates, Rights & Interests5

Forms of Ownership & Co-Ownership▾
Severalty and co-ownership

Ownership in severalty means one person or legal entity holds title. With co-ownership, two or more owners hold interests in the same property.

Tenancy in common

Each tenant in common holds an undivided interest in the whole. Shares may be equal or unequal, are transferable and inheritable, and have no automatic survivorship.

Joint tenancy

Joint tenancy is associated with the right of survivorship and traditionally the four unities of time, title, interest, and possession. At death, an interest passes to surviving joint tenant(s).

Exam Scenario
Ava owns 60% and Noah 40% as tenants in common. Noah dies. His 40% passes through his estate rather than automatically to Ava.
🎯
Tenancy in common = inheritable share. Joint tenancy = survivorship.
Freehold Estates & Bundle of Rights▾
Freehold estates

Fee simple absolute is the broadest private ownership estate: inheritable, transferable, and not limited by a special condition. A fee simple defeasible can end when a condition is violated.

Determinable vs. condition subsequent

A fee simple determinable ends automatically when its stated limitation occurs. A fee simple subject to a condition subsequent does not automatically end; the grantor generally has a right of re-entry and must act.

Life estates and future interests

A life estate lasts for a named life. When it ends, a reversion returns title to the grantor or a remainder passes title to a remainderman. A life tenant should not commit waste.

Bundle of rights

Ownership includes rights to possess, use/control, exclude, encumber, and dispose, subject to law and valid restrictions.

💡
Determinable = automatic ending. Condition subsequent = right to act and recover.
Leasehold Estates & Lease Types▾
Four leasehold estates
EstateMeaning
Estate for yearsFixed beginning and ending dates.
Periodic estateRenews for successive periods until proper notice.
Estate at willNo fixed term; possession continues with the owner's consent until properly terminated.
Estate at sufferanceHoldover after lawful possession ends, without landlord consent.
Rent structures

In a gross lease, the landlord generally pays most operating expenses. In a net lease, the tenant pays rent plus specified expenses. A percentage lease includes a percentage of business sales, often with base rent. A ground lease is a long-term lease of land.

🎯
Leasehold estate describes duration/possession; lease type describes rent and expense structure.
Liens, Priority & Property Rights▾
Lien classifications

A lien secures a debt or obligation. It can be voluntary or involuntary, and specific to identified property or general against property more broadly.

Lien priority

Priority controls payment order. The general concept is first in time, first in right, often tied to recording, but statutes create exceptions. Real estate property tax liens generally have superior priority.

Air, surface & subsurface rights

Surface rights concern the land surface; subsurface rights include mineral interests; air rights concern usable space above land. These interests may sometimes be separated, sold, or leased.

Exam Scenario
An owner sells mineral rights but keeps the house and surface estate. The ownership interests have been separated.
Deeds & Transfer of Title▾
Valid deed fundamentals

A deed conveys title. It generally identifies a competent grantor and grantee, shows intent to convey, contains an adequate legal description, and is signed by the grantor. Delivery and acceptance complete the conveyance.

Common deeds
DeedProtection
General warrantyBroad warranties, including claims arising before grantor ownership.
Special warrantyWarranties generally limited to grantor's ownership period.
Bargain and saleLimited or no express warranties depending on jurisdiction.
QuitclaimWhatever interest grantor has, if any; no title warranties.
Alienation

Voluntary alienation is intentional transfer, such as by deed or will. Involuntary alienation can occur through foreclosure, condemnation, adverse possession, or applicable intestate law.

🎯
Signing alone is not enough: watch for delivery and acceptance.
Recording, Title Evidence & Title Protection▾
Notice and recording

Actual notice is direct knowledge. Constructive notice is notice the law treats a person as having, commonly through properly recorded public information. Recording helps protect interests and gives constructive notice; it is not the same as creating a valid deed.

Evidence of title

An abstract of title summarizes recorded instruments. A chain of title traces ownership transfers. Marketable title is reasonably free of serious defects or doubt. A cloud on title is a claim or defect that may impair title.

Clearing and protecting title

An attorney may issue an opinion of title. A quiet-title action resolves competing claims or certain clouds. Title insurance protects against covered financial losses from title defects; owner's and lender's policies protect their respective insured interests.

💡
Evidence finds problems. Quiet title can resolve claims. Title insurance covers specified financial risk.

Pearson VUE allocates 11 of the 80 scored National/General sales questions to this section. “≈ 11 exam questions” is an exam-weight guide, not a score or guarantee of the exact questions you will see.

Cognitive weighting
Knowledge6
Application3
Analysis2
Subsection weighting
Concept of Value4
Appraisal Process2
Methods / CMA / BPO5
Concept of Value & Principles▾
Market value, market price, cost and investment value

Market value is an opinion of the most probable price a property should bring under typical, competitive, arm's-length conditions when buyer and seller are knowledgeable, acting voluntarily, and the property has been adequately exposed to the market. Market price is the amount actually paid in a specific transaction. The two can be different because a sale may involve unusual motivation, special financing, family relationships, or limited exposure.

Cost is the amount required to create or acquire an improvement. Cost does not automatically equal value. Investment value is the value of a property to a particular investor based on that investor's goals, financing, risk tolerance, and expected return.

Exam distinction
A property can sell for $390,000 even if an appraiser concludes its market value is $380,000. The $390,000 is the market price; $380,000 is the appraiser's opinion of market value.
The four characteristics of value; DUST

A property tends to have value when four conditions exist: Demand; people want it and have purchasing power; Utility; it serves a useful purpose; Scarcity; supply is limited relative to demand; and Transferability; ownership rights can be transferred.

💡
DUST = Demand · Utility · Scarcity · Transferability. Do not confuse DUST with the physical/economic characteristics of real estate from Section I.
Core principles of value

Substitution: a buyer will not usually pay more for a property than the cost of an equally desirable substitute. Supply and demand: value tends to rise when demand increases while supply remains limited. Highest and best use: the use that is legally permissible, physically possible, financially feasible, and maximally productive. Conformity: value is generally supported when a property is similar to surrounding properties. Contribution: an improvement is worth what it adds to overall property value, not necessarily what it cost.

Progression describes a lower-value property benefiting from more valuable surrounding properties. Regression describes a higher-value property being pulled downward by lower-value surrounding properties. Anticipation means value is influenced by expected future benefits. Competition explains why unusually high profits attract competing supply. Change reminds you that neighborhoods, markets, regulations, and property conditions are never static.

🎯
When an exam question asks what a feature is worth, think contribution. When it asks why a buyer will not overpay compared with similar alternatives, think substitution.
Appraisal Process & Federal Oversight▾
Why an appraisal is performed

An appraisal is a professional opinion of value developed for a stated purpose and effective date. Appraisals may support lending decisions, sales, taxation disputes, estates, insurance decisions, litigation, or investment analysis. The appraiser's job is to analyze evidence and develop an independent, supportable opinion; not to "hit" a contract price.

The appraisal process

A typical appraisal assignment follows a logical sequence: identify the appraisal problem and intended use; determine the scope of work; collect and verify relevant market and property data; identify the property's highest and best use; apply the appropriate valuation approaches; reconcile the indications of value; and report the final opinion.

Reconciliation is not averaging
The appraiser does not simply average three approach results. Reconciliation weighs the reliability and relevance of the available data and methods for that specific property and assignment.
Federal oversight and appraisal independence

Federal law and regulation shape appraisal standards for many federally related real-estate transactions. The Appraisal Subcommittee (ASC) monitors the state appraisal regulatory programs and The Appraisal Foundation. The Appraisal Foundation supports appraisal standards and qualifications through its boards, including standards commonly associated with USPAP; the Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal Practice.

For exam purposes, remember the principle of appraisal independence: lenders, agents, owners, and other interested parties should not pressure an appraiser to reach a predetermined value. The appraiser must remain impartial and follow applicable standards.

🎯
If a lender or agent tells an appraiser, "We need this to come in at $425,000," the problem is pressure on appraisal independence. An appraiser may consider legitimate new market data, but should not be coerced into a target value.
Sales Comparison Approach▾
Sales comparison approach

The sales comparison approach estimates value by comparing the subject property with recently sold comparable properties. It is especially important for owner-occupied residential property because buyers commonly compare alternatives before deciding what to pay.

The appraiser selects comparable sales, verifies the transaction data, identifies meaningful differences, and adjusts the comparables to make them more like the subject. Adjustments are made to the comparable, not to the subject.

The direction of adjustments

If a comparable is superior to the subject on a value-relevant feature, subtract from the comparable's sale price. If the comparable is inferior, add to the comparable. A useful question is: What would this comparable likely have sold for if it had the same relevant characteristics as the subject?

Example
A comparable sold for $410,000 and has a garage worth $20,000 more than the subject's parking arrangement. Because the comparable is superior, subtract $20,000. Its adjusted indication is $390,000.
Common comparison elements

Adjustments may reflect property rights conveyed, financing or sale conditions, market conditions or date of sale, location, site characteristics, size, quality, condition, age, bedroom/bath count, garages, pools, views, and other features that the market recognizes.

💡
Comparable superior? Subtract. Comparable inferior? Add. The goal is to make the comparable resemble the subject.
🎯
The sales comparison approach is driven by market evidence. Do not confuse it with the cost approach's replacement-cost calculations or the income approach's capitalization of income.
Cost Approach & Depreciation▾
Cost approach

The cost approach estimates value by considering the value of the land plus the current cost of the improvements, less accrued depreciation. A simplified relationship is: Land value + cost new − depreciation = indicated value.

This approach is often useful for newer structures and special-purpose properties when good comparable sales or income data are limited.

Reproduction cost vs. replacement cost

Reproduction cost is the cost to create an exact duplicate using the same or essentially identical materials, design, and workmanship. Replacement cost is the cost to build a structure with equivalent utility using current materials, standards, design, and construction methods.

Three categories of depreciation

Physical deterioration is loss in value from wear, age, damage, or deferred maintenance. Functional obsolescence is loss in value caused by a design or feature that no longer meets market expectations; for example, an awkward floor plan. External (economic) obsolescence is loss in value caused by influences outside the property, such as a nearby heavy industrial use or persistent external noise.

Curable vs. incurable
An item is generally curable when the expected increase in value justifies the cost to correct it. It is generally incurable when correction is impractical or costs more than the value it would add.
🎯
External obsolescence originates outside the property and is usually beyond the owner's control. A worn roof is physical deterioration; a badly outdated layout is functional obsolescence.
Income Approach, GRM & GIM▾
Income approach

The income approach estimates value from the income-producing ability of a property. It is especially relevant to investment property because investors commonly relate value to expected income and return.

NOI and capitalization rate

Net operating income (NOI) is income remaining after allowable operating expenses are deducted from effective gross income, but before debt service and income taxes. The basic direct-capitalization relationship is Value = NOI ÷ capitalization rate. Rearranged: Cap rate = NOI ÷ Value and NOI = Value × Cap rate.

Income capitalization
Value = NOI ÷ Cap Rate
Cap rates are expressed as decimals in the formula. Example: 8% = 0.08.
Gross rent multiplier and gross income multiplier

A gross rent multiplier (GRM) is commonly used with rental income, particularly residential rentals: Value = Monthly Rent × GRM when the GRM was developed from comparable market data using monthly rent. A gross income multiplier (GIM) uses gross income rather than net income and is often associated with larger income properties.

GRM is not a cap rate
GRM/GIM use gross income figures and do not directly deduct operating expenses. Direct capitalization uses NOI and a capitalization rate.
🎯
Do not subtract mortgage payments when calculating NOI for a capitalization problem. Debt service is a financing expense, not an operating expense of the real estate itself.
CMA, BPO, Assessed Value & Taxes▾
CMA, BPO and appraisal; know the difference

A Comparative Market Analysis (CMA) is commonly prepared by a real estate licensee to help a seller choose a listing price or help a buyer evaluate an offering price. It analyzes competing, active, pending, expired, and recently sold properties as appropriate to the assignment. A CMA is not automatically an appraisal.

A Broker Price Opinion (BPO) is a broker's or qualified licensee's opinion of a property's probable selling price, often requested for specific business purposes. Whether and when a licensee may perform a BPO can depend on state law and the nature of the assignment. A BPO is distinct from an appraisal performed by a licensed or certified appraiser.

ToolTypical purposePrepared by
AppraisalFormal opinion of value for an identified assignmentLicensed/certified appraiser when required
CMAAssist with listing or offering strategyReal estate licensee
BPOOpinion of probable selling price for an allowed business purposeBroker/qualified licensee subject to law
Assessed value and property-tax implications

Assessed value is the value placed on property by a taxing authority for property-tax purposes. It may differ from market value. Property tax is commonly calculated by applying the jurisdiction's tax rate to the taxable or assessed value after applicable rules and exemptions.

Exam idea
A home can have an assessed value of $310,000, a recent market-value opinion of $350,000, and an actual sale price of $357,500. These numbers measure different things and do not have to be equal.
🎯
When the question asks for an opinion of market value for lending, think appraisal. When it asks for a licensee's pricing analysis for listing strategy, think CMA.

Financing & Mortgages

Module 4; The Word for This Module
“The rich ruleth over the poor, and the borrower is servant to the lender.”
Proverbs 22:7
Understanding debt with clear eyes is wisdom. Learn financing so you can guide clients honestly through the biggest obligation most will ever sign.
Mortgage Instruments & Clauses▾
The note and the security

Two documents work together. The promissory note is the borrower's promise to repay; the actual debt. The mortgage (or deed of trust) is the security instrument that pledges the property as collateral. If the borrower defaults, the security instrument allows foreclosure.

Mortgage vs. deed of trust
MortgageDeed of trust
PartiesBorrower (mortgagor) & lender (mortgagee)Borrower (trustor), lender (beneficiary) & trustee
ForeclosureUsually judicialOften non-judicial (power of sale)
Key clauses

An acceleration clause lets the lender demand the entire balance on default. A due-on-sale (alienation) clause requires payoff if the property is sold, preventing loan assumption without approval. A prepayment clause governs early payoff penalties. A defeasance clause requires the lender to release the lien once the loan is paid.

💡
Note = the promise to pay (the debt). Mortgage/deed of trust = the pledge of the property (the security). The note follows the borrower; the lien follows the land.
🎯
A due-on-sale clause blocks a buyer from simply assuming the loan; the lender must consent. An acceleration clause is what makes foreclosure of the whole balance possible.
Loan Types & Programs▾
Conventional vs. government-backed

A conventional loan is not insured or guaranteed by the government. If the down payment is under 20% (loan-to-value above 80%), the lender usually requires private mortgage insurance (PMI), which can be removed as equity builds.

ProgramBackingSignature feature
FHAInsured by the Federal Housing AdministrationLow down payment (as little as 3.5%); MIP required
VAGuaranteed by the Dept. of Veterans Affairs0% down for eligible veterans; funding fee
USDAGuaranteed by the Dept. of AgricultureRural areas; low/no down payment
Amortized vs. other structures

A fully amortized loan pays principal and interest so the balance reaches zero at the end. A term (straight) loan pays interest only with principal due at the end (a balloon). An adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) has a rate that changes with an index. A package loan includes personal property; a blanket loan covers several parcels with a partial release clause.

💡
FHA insures (MIP) and VA guarantees; the government does not lend the money itself; approved lenders do. VA loans can reach 100% financing.
🎯
PMI (conventional) is different from MIP (FHA). PMI can be canceled as equity grows; FHA MIP often lasts the life of the loan depending on the down payment.
Financing Concepts & the Market▾
Primary vs. secondary market

The primary market is where borrowers get loans from lenders (banks, credit unions, mortgage companies). The secondary market is where those loans are bought and sold, replenishing lenders' funds. Key players: Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac buy loans; Ginnie Mae backs government-insured loans.

The Federal Reserve

The Fed influences the cost and supply of money through the discount rate, reserve requirements, and open-market operations. Tightening money tends to raise rates and slow lending; loosening does the opposite. The Fed does not set mortgage rates directly.

Points, LTV, and equity

A discount point equals 1% of the loan amount, paid up front to lower the interest rate (buying down the rate). Loan-to-value (LTV) is loan ÷ value; a lower LTV means more borrower equity and less lender risk.

💡
Fannie & Freddie = the secondary market that keeps money flowing back to lenders. The Fed = the referee of money supply, not the source of your mortgage.
🎯
One point = 1% of the LOAN amount, not the price. Points paid to lower the rate are 'buying down' the loan.
Federal Lending Laws▾
Truth in Lending Act (TILA) & Regulation Z

TILA, implemented by Regulation Z, requires lenders to disclose the true cost of credit, including the annual percentage rate (APR) and finance charges, so borrowers can compare loans. It governs certain advertising: if an ad states a specific credit term (a rate or payment), it must disclose the other required terms (a 'trigger term' rule). It also gives a right of rescission on certain refinances of a primary residence.

RESPA

The Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act covers federally related mortgage loans. It requires a Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure, prohibits kickbacks and unearned fees for referrals, and limits escrow amounts.

ECOA

The Equal Credit Opportunity Act prohibits discrimination in lending based on race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, age, or receipt of public assistance.

💡
TILA/Reg Z = disclose the COST of credit (APR). RESPA = govern the SETTLEMENT process and ban kickbacks. ECOA = ban discrimination in CREDIT decisions.
🎯
A vague ad ('great rates!') has no trigger terms and needs no extra disclosure. Stating a specific figure (like '5% APR' or '$900/month') triggers full Reg Z disclosure.

Valuation, Appraisal & Market Analysis

Module 5; The Word for This Module
“A just weight and balance are the Lord's.”
Proverbs 16:11
Valuation is the discipline of telling the truth about worth. Weigh honestly, and your numbers will serve people rather than mislead them.
Principles & Characteristics of Value▾
The four characteristics of value; DUST

For anything to have value in the market, four elements must be present, remembered as DUST:

DDemand; desire plus purchasing power
UUtility; usefulness for a purpose
SScarcity; limited supply
TTransferability; ability to convey title
Key principles
PrincipleMeaning
Highest & best useThe legal, physical, and financial use that gives the greatest value
SubstitutionA buyer pays no more than the cost of an equally desirable substitute
ConformityValue is maximized when a property conforms to its surroundings
Progression / RegressionA modest home gains value near better homes; a fine home loses value near lesser ones
Supply & demandValue rises when demand exceeds supply
Types of value

Market value is the most probable price a willing buyer and seller would agree to under normal conditions. It differs from market price (what actually sold) and cost (dollars to build). Assessed value is for taxation; insured value is for coverage.

💡
Substitution is the backbone of the sales-comparison approach: buyers won't pay more than a comparable alternative costs.
🎯
Market value is an OPINION of the most probable price under normal terms; not the same as the price a specific property actually sold for (market price).
The Three Approaches to Value▾
Sales comparison approach

The appraiser compares the subject to recently sold comparables and adjusts for differences. The rule: adjust the comparable, never the subject. If a comp is superior, subtract; if inferior, add. This approach is best for single-family homes and relies on the principle of substitution.

Cost approach

Value = land value + (cost to rebuild the improvements − depreciation). Best for new or special-purpose properties (schools, churches) that rarely sell.

Income approach

Used for income-producing property. The core formula ties income, rate, and value:

Worked Example
Value = Net Operating Income ÷ Capitalization Rate. If a building earns $60,000 NOI and the market cap rate is 8%, value = $60,000 ÷ 0.08 = $750,000. A quicker screen for small residential rentals is the Gross Rent Multiplier (GRM) = price ÷ gross rent.
💡
CBS: Cost for new/special-purpose, By-comparison (sales) for homes, Stream of income for rentals.
🎯
Adjust the COMPARABLE, not the subject. Comp better than the subject → subtract; comp worse → add. Reversing this is the most common exam trap.
The Appraisal Process, Depreciation & CMA▾
Depreciation; three kinds
TypeCauseCurable?
Physical deteriorationWear and tear, ageOften curable
Functional obsolescenceOutdated design or featuresSometimes curable
External (economic) obsolescenceOff-site factors (highway, declining area)Incurable; outside the property
External obsolescence is always incurable
Because the cause lies outside the property line; a new landfill next door, a downturn in the local economy; the owner cannot fix it. That distinguishes it from physical and functional problems.
Appraisal vs. CMA vs. BPO

An appraisal is an independent, licensed opinion of value. A comparative market analysis (CMA) is prepared by a licensee to help price a listing; it is not an appraisal. A broker price opinion (BPO) is similar. Reconciliation is the appraiser's weighing of the approaches into a final opinion; never a simple average.

💡
Depreciation for appraisal = loss in value from ANY cause. Depreciation for taxes is a separate accounting write-off; don't mix the two on the exam.
🎯
Only physical and functional problems inside the property can be curable. Anything caused by factors OUTSIDE the property (external/economic obsolescence) is incurable.

Clear Records. Fair Practice. Texas Responsibility.
DALLAS · TEXAS

Title, Fair Housing & Texas Disclosures

Module 6; The Word for This Module
“In righteousness shalt thou judge thy neighbour.”
Leviticus 19:15
Fair dealing is not merely the law here; it is the heart of it. Learn these rules as the shape justice takes in a transaction.
Deeds & Transfer of Title▾
What a valid deed requires

A deed transfers title from the grantor to the grantee. Requirements generally include: a competent grantor, a named grantee, consideration, a granting clause (words of conveyance), an accurate legal description, and the grantor's signature and delivery and acceptance. The grantee need not sign.

Types of deeds; by warranty
DeedProtection to grantee
General warrantyGreatest; grantor defends title against all claims, ever
Special warrantyGrantor warrants only against claims during their ownership
Bargain and saleImplies ownership but no warranties
QuitclaimLeast; conveys only whatever interest the grantor has, if any
Title & recording

Recording in the public records gives constructive notice to the world of one's interest. Actual notice is what a person truly knows. A clear chain of title shows ownership passing without gaps. Adverse possession can transfer title to someone who possesses land openly, notoriously, continuously, and hostilely for the statutory period.

💡
General warranty deed = the buyer's best protection. Quitclaim = the weakest, often used to clear a cloud on title, not to sell.
🎯
A deed needs the GRANTOR's signature, not the grantee's. Title passes upon delivery AND acceptance; not at signing.
Title Insurance, Closing & Prorations▾
Title insurance

A title search and abstract reveal the history of ownership and any defects. Title insurance protects against losses from covered title defects. An owner's policy protects the buyer; a lender's (mortgagee) policy protects the lender for the loan amount.

Closing / settlement

At closing, funds and documents change hands. Costs are split by custom and contract. Prorations divide ongoing items (taxes, interest, HOA dues) between buyer and seller as of the closing date. The party who used the item pays for their share.

Worked Example
Annual taxes of $3,650 prorated to the seller through day 100 of the year: $3,650 ÷ 365 = $10/day × 100 days = $1,000 charged to the seller (a credit to the buyer if the seller has not yet paid).
💡
Debit = a charge; Credit = money in your favor. The buyer is credited what the seller owes but hasn't paid; the seller is credited what they prepaid.
🎯
A lender's title policy protects the LENDER, not the buyer. Buyers need a separate owner's policy for their own protection.
Federal Fair Housing; FReSH CoRN▾
The protected classes

The federal Fair Housing Act of 1968 (expanded in 1988) prohibits discrimination in housing based on seven protected classes, remembered as FReSH CoRN:

FFamilial status (children under 18, pregnancy)
RReligion
SSex
HHandicap (disability)
CColor
RRace
NNational origin

Race was the first protected class (Civil Rights Act of 1866) and can never be exempted. The 1988 amendments added familial status and handicap.

Prohibited practices
PracticeWhat it is
SteeringDirecting buyers toward or away from areas based on a protected class
BlockbustingInducing panic selling by claiming a protected group is moving in
RedliningRefusing loans/insurance in certain areas based on protected class
Advertising
Ads may not state a preference or limitation based on a protected class. Saying a home is 'perfect for a Christian family' is illegal because it expresses a religious preference; likewise 'no children' violates familial status. Describe the property, never the desired people.
🎯
Disability rules require allowing reasonable modifications (tenant pays) and reasonable accommodations (like a service animal, even with a no-pets policy). 'Adult communities' (55+) are a narrow exemption to familial status only.
Mandated Disclosures & Practice▾
Lead-based paint

Federal law requires disclosure of known lead-based paint hazards for housing built before 1978. Sellers/landlords must give the EPA pamphlet, disclose known hazards, and offer buyers a 10-day period to test.

Environmental awareness

Agents should recognize (not remediate) hazards: asbestos, radon (a gas from soil), lead, underground storage tanks, mold, and CERCLA/Superfund liability for contamination. Wetlands and flood zones affect use and financing.

Material facts & stigmatized property

Agents must disclose known material defects that affect value or safety. Facts about a prior occupant's illness or death are often not required (and may be protected), but a licensee must answer honestly and never actively conceal a defect.

Trust accounts & advertising

Client funds must be kept in a separate trust/escrow account; never mixed with the broker's money (commingling is prohibited). Advertising must be truthful and, in most jurisdictions, identify the brokerage.

💡
Before 1978 = lead-based paint disclosure + 10-day test window. Radon comes from the ground; asbestos was used in old insulation. Know the source, not the remedy.
🎯
Commingling (mixing client funds with the broker's) and conversion (using client funds) are serious violations. Keep earnest money in the trust account, not the operating account.
Texas Special Topics; DTPA, Foreclosure & Landlord-Tenant▾

Three Texas-specific areas

DTPA
The Deceptive Trade Practices Act protects consumers from deceptive acts. Knowing violations can bring treble (triple) damages, so honesty is not just ethics; it is expensive to break.
Texas foreclosure
Texas commonly uses non-judicial foreclosure through a deed of trust with a power-of-sale clause. Foreclosure sales occur on the first Tuesday of the month. There is no right of redemption after a mortgage foreclosure (unlike a tax sale).
Landlord-tenant
No self-help evictions; a landlord cannot change locks or remove belongings without following the legal process. Security deposits must be returned within the statutory window after move-out.
💡
Memory trick. DTPA = triple damages for knowing violations. Texas foreclosure = “first Tuesday, no redemption” for mortgages. No self-help evictions.
Worked example
A landlord, frustrated with a late-paying tenant, changes the locks and sets the tenant's furniture on the curb. That is an illegal self-help eviction under Texas law; the landlord must go through the courts.
🎯
On the exam. Remember: DTPA treble damages, Texas non-judicial foreclosure on the first Tuesday with no mortgage redemption, and no self-help evictions.

Texas Law, Real Estate Math & Final Review

Module 7; The Word for This Module
“Commit thy works unto the Lord, and thy thoughts shall be established.”
Proverbs 16:3
You have carried the weight of study faithfully. Do the math calmly, trust your preparation, and commit the outcome to God.
The Core Formulas▾
Start every problem the same way

Most real estate math is one relationship: Part = Total × Rate. Cover what you want to find. Convert percentages to decimals, and always ask what unit the answer should be in.

Commission
Commission = Sale Price × Rate
Sale Pricethe selling price
Ratecommission % as a decimal
=the dollars earned
To split: total commission × the broker's share, then × the agent's share.
Percentage / Profit
New = Old × (1 ± %change)
Oldoriginal value
%changegain (+) or loss (−) as a decimal
Newresulting value
Profit % = (gain ÷ original) × 100. Watch whether the base is cost or sale price.
Loan-to-Value
LTV = Loan ÷ Value
Loanamount borrowed
Valueprice or appraised value
=ratio, as a %
Down payment % = 100% − LTV. Lower LTV = more equity, less lender risk.
Area
Area = Length × Width
Llength in feet
Wwidth in feet
=square feet
43,560 sq ft = 1 acre. For triangles, Area = ½ × base × height.
Income (Cap Rate)
Value = NOI ÷ Cap Rate
NOInet operating income
Cap Ratemarket rate as a decimal
Valueproperty value
Rearrange: NOI = Value × Rate; Rate = NOI ÷ Value.
Property Tax (Mills)
Tax = Assessed Value × Mill Rate
Assessedtaxable value
Mill1 mill = $0.001 = $1 per $1,000
Taxannual tax owed
A 25-mill rate = 0.025. Assessed value may be a % of market value.
💡
Points: 1 point = 1% of the LOAN. Prorations: annual amount ÷ 365 = daily rate, then × days.
Worked Examples; See the Process▾
Commission split
Worked Example
A $320,000 home sells at 6%. The listing broker and buyer's broker split 50/50, and the listing agent keeps 60% of their broker's half. Total = $320,000 × 0.06 = $19,200. Listing side = $9,600. Listing agent = $9,600 × 0.60 = $5,760.
Profit on a sale
Worked Example
An investor buys at $150,000, spends $20,000, and sells at $204,000. Cost basis = $170,000. Profit = $34,000. Profit % = $34,000 ÷ $170,000 = 20%.
Proration
Worked Example
Seller owes taxes of $4,380/year and closes on day 90 (having paid nothing). Daily = $4,380 ÷ 365 = $12. Seller's share = $12 × 90 = $1,080 (debit seller / credit buyer).
Net to seller
Worked Example
A seller wants $188,000 net after a 6% commission (no other costs). Sale price = $188,000 ÷ (1 − 0.06) = $188,000 ÷ 0.94 = $200,000.
💡
For 'net to seller' problems, DIVIDE by (1 − rate). Do NOT just add the commission percentage to the net; that gives the wrong number.
🎯
Read the base carefully: commission and points are on different numbers (sale price vs. loan). Mixing the bases is the top math error on the exam.
Final Review; Acronyms, Numbers & Strategy▾
Every acronym on one page
AcronymStands for
MARIAFixture tests: Method, Adaptability, Relationship, Intention, Agreement
PETEGovernment powers: Police power, Eminent domain, Taxation, Escheat
TTIPFour unities of joint tenancy: Time, Title, Interest, Possession
OLD CARFiduciary duties: Obedience, Loyalty, Disclosure, Confidentiality, Accounting, Reasonable care
COLEValid contract: Consideration, Offer/acceptance, Legal purpose, (competent) parties
DUSTValue: Demand, Utility, Scarcity, Transferability
FReSH CoRNProtected classes: Familial, Religion, Sex, Handicap, Color, Race, National origin
Critical national numbers
NumberMeaning
1866Civil Rights Act; race, never exempt
1968 / 1988Fair Housing Act / amendments (added familial & handicap)
1978Lead-based paint disclosure threshold; 10-day test window
43,560Square feet in one acre
1 point1% of the loan amount
80% LTVAbove this, conventional loans usually need PMI
3.5% / 0%FHA minimum down / VA down for eligible veterans
Exam-day strategy

Read the last line of the question first; it tells you what is actually being asked. Eliminate two wrong answers before choosing. For 'EXCEPT' and 'NOT' questions, flip your thinking. Do the easy questions first and flag the rest. Trust your preparation; do not change answers without a clear reason.

🎯
When two answers seem right, choose the one that is MORE complete or MORE specific to what the last line asks. Watch for absolute words like 'always' and 'never.'
TREC, TRELA & Commission Powers▾

Law vs. regulator

TRELA is the Texas Real Estate License Act; the LAW. TREC is the Texas Real Estate Commission; the REGULATOR that enforces the law. The lens for every state answer is public protection.

What TREC CAN do
Investigate complaints, suspend or revoke licenses, impose administrative fines, and require education. TREC's job is to protect the public.
What TREC CANNOT do
TREC cannot send anyone to jail and cannot directly award money damages to a wronged consumer; those come from the courts.
💡
Memory trick. TREC can discipline your license; the courts handle jail and money damages. “Public protection” is the answer to close state questions.

A sales agent must always work under a sponsoring broker, and all compensation flows through that broker. Entity brokerages must have a designated broker.

Worked example
A consumer complains that an agent misrepresented a property. TREC investigates and can suspend the agent's license and fine them; but if the consumer wants money back, they must sue in court. TREC does not hand out damages.
🎯
On the exam. Know the split: TREC = discipline/education/fines; courts = jail and damages. All pay goes through the sponsoring broker.
Licensing Requirements; Know Every Number▾

The numbers TREC will test

RequirementNumber
Pre-license education180 classroom hours
Passing score (each portion)70% on national AND 70% on state
Background checkRequired
RenewalContinuing education required
💡
Memory trick. 180 pre-license hours. 70% to pass; and you must pass BOTH the national and state portions separately.

You must pass each portion on its own. A great national score cannot rescue a failing state score, and vice versa. A background check (fingerprints) is required, and continuing education keeps the license active at renewal.

Worked example
A candidate scores 85% national but 65% state. Did they pass? No; each portion needs 70% independently. They keep the passing national portion (within the allowed window) and retake only the state portion.
🎯
On the exam. 180 hours and 70%/70% are frequent recall items. Remember the two portions are scored separately.
Recovery Trust Fund; Critical Numbers▾

A safety net funded by license holders

The Real Estate Recovery Trust Fund pays consumers who win a court judgment against a license holder but cannot collect it. Memorize the caps; they are pure recall points.

CapAmount
Maximum per transaction$50,000
Maximum per license holder (lifetime)$100,000
💡
Memory trick. Recovery Fund: $50,000 per transaction, $100,000 per license holder. “Win in court first, then apply.”
How it works
The consumer must first win a court judgment, then apply to the fund when the licensee cannot pay. When the fund pays out, the licensee's license is automatically revoked. The licensee must repay the fund with interest before ever being relicensed.
Worked example
A buyer wins a $65,000 judgment against an agent for fraud, but the agent has no money. The buyer applies to the Recovery Trust Fund. The per-transaction cap is $50,000, so the fund pays $50,000. The agent's license is automatically revoked and cannot be restored until the fund is repaid with interest.
🎯
On the exam. These numbers are almost guaranteed: $50,000 per transaction, $100,000 per license holder. Payment triggers automatic revocation.
License Exemptions Under TRELA▾

Who does NOT need a license

Some people can perform real-estate-like acts without a license because they are acting in another recognized capacity.

Exempt partyWhy
Property ownersActing on their own behalf with their own property
AttorneysActing within the practice of law
Court-appointed fiduciariesExecutors, receivers, bankruptcy trustees acting under court order
Government employeesActing in their official capacity
💡
Memory trick. Owners for themselves, attorneys in practice, court-appointed fiduciaries under order, and government employees on the job; no license needed.
Worked example
A bankruptcy trustee, appointed by a court, sells a debtor's property as part of the case. No real estate license is required, because the trustee acts under a court order as a fiduciary; a recognized TRELA exemption.
🎯
On the exam. Exemptions require acting in the recognized capacity. An owner selling their own property is exempt; an owner selling a neighbor's property for a fee is not.

Vocabulary & Memory Tools

Fixture
Personal property permanently attached so it becomes real property.
Emblements
Annual crops treated as the tenant farmer's personal property.
Fee simple absolute
The greatest estate: full ownership, indefinite and inheritable.
Life estate
Ownership limited to the duration of a person's life.
Joint tenancy
Co-ownership with the right of survivorship and four unities.
Tenancy in common
Co-ownership without survivorship; shares are inheritable.
Easement appurtenant
A use-right that benefits an adjoining parcel and runs with the land.
Encroachment
An unauthorized physical intrusion onto another's property.
Eminent domain
The government's power to take private land for public use with compensation.
Escheat
Reversion of property to the state when an owner dies with no heirs or will.
Fiduciary
One who owes duties of trust (OLD CAR) to a principal/client.
Dual agency
Representing both parties; legal only with informed written consent.
Procuring cause
The broker whose efforts actually produced the ready, willing, able buyer.
Equitable title
The buyer's interest in property after signing but before closing.
Contingency
A condition that must be met or the contract may be canceled.
Novation
Substituting a new contract or party, releasing the original party.
Specific performance
A court order compelling completion of the agreed sale.
Counteroffer
A response that rejects and replaces the original offer.
Statute of Frauds
Law requiring real estate contracts to be in writing to be enforceable.
Liquidated damages
Damages agreed in advance, often the earnest money on breach.
Fixture
Personal property that has become permanently attached to real property.
Appurtenance
A right that belongs to and passes with the land.
Fee simple absolute
The fullest form of ownership, unlimited in duration with no conditions.
Life estate
Ownership measured by someone's lifetime.
Remainderman
The person who receives title when a life estate ends.
Joint tenancy
Co-ownership with the right of survivorship and four unities.
Tenancy in common
Co-ownership with no survivorship and possibly unequal shares.
Encroachment
A physical intrusion onto a neighbor's land.
Escheat
The state taking title when an owner dies with no will and no heirs.
Homestead
A family's primary residence protected from most creditors in Texas.
Fiduciary
One who owes duties of trust and loyalty to a principal.
Principal
The client who hires the broker.
Special agent
An agent hired for one specific transaction.
General agent
An agent authorized to handle ongoing matters, like a property manager.
Promissory note
The borrower's written promise to repay the debt.
Deed of trust
A security instrument using a trustee, allowing non-judicial foreclosure.
Acceleration clause
Lets the lender demand the full balance upon default.
Loan-to-value (LTV)
Loan amount divided by property value.
Discount point
A fee equal to 1% of the loan, paid to lower the interest rate.
Amortization
Gradual loan payoff of principal and interest over time.
Cap rate
Net operating income divided by value; the income-approach rate.
Market value
The most probable price under normal, arm's-length conditions.
Depreciation
Loss in value from physical, functional, or external causes.
External obsolescence
Incurable loss in value from causes outside the property.
